itens.resumo: Sixteenth ecumenical council (1414-1418): it ended the Great Western Schism by electing Martin V and condemned the Bohemian reformer Jan Hus as a heretic, besides leaving the conciliarist decrees «Haec Sancta» and «Frequens».
itens.corpo:
Gathered in the imperial city of Constance, in present-day Germany, between November 5, 1414 and April 22, 1418, under the direct patronage of King Sigismund of Luxembourg — then King of the Romans and future emperor of the Holy Roman Empire —, the council was convoked with the primary aim of ending the Great Western Schism, which since 1378 had divided Latin Christendom among rival papal obediences. At the time of its opening, three men simultaneously claimed the papacy: Gregory XII, of the Roman line, who was the legitimate pope; Benedict XIII, of the Avignon line; and John XXIII, heir of the line elected by the failed Council of Pisa (1409). Gathered with the intention of healing the schism, the Council of Pisa had ended up aggravating it, for, by deposing the two existing pontiffs, who refused to cooperate, it elected a third, Alexander V; Christendom then had three simultaneous popes, and Pisa was never recognized as a valid council by canonists or theologians.

Over its forty-five general sessions, with some 600 participants present, the council obtained the voluntary resignation of Gregory XII — who, before resigning, by means of two bulls of March 13, 1415 («Terrenas Affectiones» and «Cum ad laudem»), conferred on his legate Carlo Malatesta the power to formally convoke the council in order to preserve the juridical continuity of the Roman succession; this convocation and the effective resignation took place on July 4, 1415, the date from which the council came to be regarded as ecumenical —, deposed John XXIII, who had been captured after a failed attempt to flee in disguise — he was even imprisoned and later freed by Martin V —, and, not managing to obtain the resignation of Benedict XIII, isolated in his castle of Peñíscola and who would die in 1423 still proclaiming himself the legitimate pope, simply disregarded his authority. Free of the three claimants, the council gathered in conclave and, on November 11, 1417 — in the only papal election held outside the Italian peninsula since the end of the Avignon exile —, elected the Roman cardinal Oddone Colonna, who took the name Martin V, restoring a single papacy recognized throughout western Europe. About two thirds of the sessions (those numbered 14 to 45) were later ratified by the pope, while the first thirteen — held before the convocation by Gregory XII — were declared null by him.

Alongside the resolution of the schism, the council tried the Bohemian theologian Jan Hus, rector of the University of Prague, whose ideas — influenced by the Englishman John Wycliffe — criticized the wealth and corruption of the clergy and upheld the supreme authority of Scripture over ecclesiastical tradition. Summoned under a safe-conduct from Sigismund himself, Hus traveled voluntarily to Constance in October 1414, but was arrested a few weeks after his arrival, under pressure from the local clergy, who considered the safe-conduct invalid in matters of heresy. Tried and condemned, he refused to recant and was handed over to the secular arm, being burned alive on July 6, 1415. The council also condemned, posthumously, the writings of John Wycliffe, who had died decades earlier, ordering the exhumation and public burning of his remains — an order carried out only in 1428. The execution of Hus, seen in Bohemia as a betrayal of the royal word, set off the bloody Hussite Wars (1419-1434), which began with the First Defenestration of Prague and would end only with the defeat of the radical Taborites at the battle of Lipany, anticipating by more than a century central themes that the Protestant Reformation would take up again with Luther.

From the standpoint of Catholic ecclesiology, Constance also left an ambiguous and lasting theological legacy. Its decree «Haec Sancta» (Session V, April 6, 1415) — approved in the vacuum left by the flight of John XXIII — affirms that the council, «legitimately assembled in the Holy Spirit», receives its power directly from Christ and that everyone, «including the pope», owes it obedience in matters of faith, the eradication of the schism, and the reform of the Church «in head and members»; and the decree «Frequens» (October 9, 1417) ordered the periodic convocation of future councils — one within five years, another after seven and, thereafter, every ten. These texts fed for decades the conciliarist movement, the thesis that an ecumenical council would have authority superior to that of the pope himself even in matters of faith, whose most radical expression would appear in the Council of Basel (1431-1449). The Catholic reception of «Haec Sancta» remains controversial: part of the historiography and theology maintains that it was not duly approved by Martin V — who ratified the council by the bull «Inter cunctas» (February 22, 1418) with the restrictive formula «in favorem fidei et salutem animarum», without explicitly repudiating the decree — and that, for this reason, it would not form part of the council's magisterium; in the sixteenth century, the Fifth Lateran Council would seek explicitly to overcome this doctrine. Constance was also the first ecumenical council held in territory of the Holy Roman Empire, and in it Spain appears for the first time designated as a nation (Natio Hispanica).

itens.resumo: Seventeenth ecumenical council (1431-1445): it sought, with ephemeral success, union between the Latin Church and the Eastern Churches, among them the Greek and Armenian Churches.
itens.corpo:
Convoked by Martin V shortly before his death, and effectively opened under his successor Eugene IV on July 25, 1431, in the Swiss city of Basel, the council arose directly from the commitment made by the decree «Frequens» of the Council of Constance, which had established the periodic convocation of general councils. From the beginning, however, the assembly of Basel entered into open and prolonged conflict with Pope Eugene IV: the majority of the conciliar fathers gathered there maintained, in line with the conciliarism that Constance had left as an ambiguous legacy, the superiority of the authority of the council over that of the pope himself, even in matters of faith and government of the Church. When Eugene IV tried to dissolve the council in 1431, the majority of the conciliar fathers refused to obey, and the conflict would drag on for years, culminating in the formal deposition of Eugene IV by the radicals of Basel and in the election of an antipope, Amadeus VIII, Duke of Savoy, who took the name Felix V (1439-1449), prolonging in Basel a dissident council that would become increasingly irrelevant and isolated.

The part of the council that remained faithful to Eugene IV and that the Catholic Church recognizes as legitimate was transferred by papal decision to Ferrara in 1438, and then to Florence in 1439, partly because of a plague epidemic that threatened Ferrara, and partly because the wealthy city of Florence was willing to finance the conciliar work generously; between 1442 and 1445, the last sessions took place in Rome, at the Lateran.

The central and most ambitious goal of the Ferrara-Florence phase was union with the Eastern Christian Churches, separated from Rome for centuries. Seeking this reconciliation with renewed urgency in the face of the growing threat of the Ottoman Turkish advance on what remained of the Byzantine Empire, Emperor John VIII Palaiologos traveled personally to Italy, accompanied by Patriarch Joseph II of Constantinople, who would die during the conciliar proceedings, and by a delegation of Greek theologians and bishops. After months of intense theological debates on the Filioque, purgatory and the papal primacy, the decree «Laetentur Caeli» was finally signed on July 6, 1439, solemnly sealing the union with the Greeks: the Byzantine representatives accepted the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son and recognized the primacy of the Bishop of Rome; only the theologian and bishop Mark of Ephesus (Mark Eugenikos) flatly refused to sign the agreement, later becoming, in the Orthodox tradition, a symbol of resistance to the imposed union.

In the following years, similar unions, though of varying scope and duration, were concluded with other Eastern Christian communities: with the Armenians in November 1439, despite the later deposition of the Armenian catholicos who had supported the agreement; and with the Egyptian Copts and the Ethiopians in 1442, broadening the ecumenical scope of the council to communities that went back to the very Christian antiquity of Egypt and Ethiopia.

Despite the immediate diplomatic success, the union with the Greeks was never genuinely accepted by the clergy and people of Constantinople, who saw it as a theological concession imposed by political necessity in the face of the Ottoman threat, and it came definitively undone in practice after the fall of Constantinople itself to the Turks in 1453 — a political collapse that, in the eyes of many Byzantines, seemed to confirm that the religious union had not brought the Western military aid that had been expected of it. The council also produced, at the session in Florence, the important decree «Cantate Domino» (1442), which set out in a systematic way the Catholic doctrine on the seven sacraments and on the necessity of the Church for salvation.

itens.resumo: Eighteenth ecumenical council (1512-1517), the last before the Protestant Reformation: it responded to the schismatic synod of Pisa, defined the immortality of the soul, and approved the Concordat of Bologna.
itens.corpo:
The convocation of the Fifth Lateran Council was a response to a bold political and ecclesiastical maneuver. In 1511, King Louis XII of France, in military and diplomatic conflict with Pope Julius II — who had struck him with the interdict after his abandonment of the League of Cambrai —, sponsored, together with a small group of dissident cardinals, the convocation of a council at Pisa, which sought to revive the conciliarist thesis of Constance in order to judge and possibly depose the pope himself. The synod, opened at Pisa in November 1511 with only four cardinals — Bernardino López de Carvajal, Federico Sanseverino, Guillaume Briçonnet, and René de Prie — and about eighteen bishops and abbots, mostly French, was successively transferred to Milan, Asti, and Lyon, and dissolved in June 1512 without any practical result. Julius II reacted by excommunicating the rebel cardinals and convoking his own council, opened in the Basilica of Saint John Lateran, in Rome, on May 3, 1512, with the explicit aim of stripping the rival assembly of legitimacy and reaffirming papal authority over any council; Louis XII himself would eventually recognize the Lateran council and declare the conciliabulum of Pisa schismatic.

After the death of Julius II in February 1513, the proceedings continued under his successor, Pope Leo X, over the course of twelve sessions, until the solemn closing on March 16, 1517 — only a few months before Martin Luther made his 95 Theses public in Wittenberg, in October of that same year, a chronological coincidence that later historiography would not fail to note.

The council formally annulled all the decrees of the dissident synod of Pisa and clearly reaffirmed the jurisdictional superiority of the pope over any general council, seeking to put a definitive end to the theological ambiguity that the conciliarist decrees of Constance had left open almost a century earlier. In the eighth session, on December 19, 1513, by the bull «Apostolici Regiminis», the council defined as a dogma of faith the personal immortality of each human soul and its individual and direct creation by God, condemning three propositions as heretical: that the soul is mortal; that all human beings share a single common soul; and the so-called doctrine of the «double truth», according to which a proposition could be true in terms of rational philosophy even while disagreeing with revealed truth. The measure targeted currents of Averroist inspiration then widespread in certain Italian university circles. The philosopher Pietro Pomponazzi, who discussed the mortality of the soul from a purely philosophical perspective, would only publish his treatise «De immortalitate animae» in 1516, three years after the bull, and, although never condemned for heresy — having been protected by the Venetian cardinal Pietro Bembo —, he was accused of heterodoxy and forced by Leo X, in 1518, to retract.

The council also dealt with questions of a practical and disciplinary nature. In 1516 it approved the Concordat of Bologna, negotiated with the new king of France, Francis I, which regulated relations between the Holy See and the French Crown and replaced the old «Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges», giving the French monarchy considerable control over ecclesiastical appointments in its territory. It established the requirement of prior ecclesiastical license («imprimatur») for the publication of any book dealing with faith or theology, anticipating by decades the system of censorship that the Counter-Reformation would generalize, and produced reform decrees on the formation of the clergy and the discipline of preaching, without, however, attaining the depth and scope that the growing crisis of the Church demanded.

The insufficiency of the reform measures approved at Lateran V is pointed out almost unanimously by historians as one of the factors that left the Church unprepared for the shock of the Protestant Reformation, which would erupt with full force only a few months after the council's close. The broader and deeper disciplinary reform, already demanded for decades by many participants in the Lateran council itself, would come only decades later, and under much more acute pressure, with the Council of Trent (1545-1563).

itens.resumo: Twentieth ecumenical council (1869-1870): defined the dogma of papal infallibility in the constitution «Pastor Aeternus» and was suspended by the occupation of Rome.
itens.corpo:
Convoked by Pope Pius IX through the bull «Aeterni Patris» of June 29, 1868, the First Vatican Council opened solemnly in Saint Peter's Basilica, in the Vatican, on December 8, 1869, gathering between seven hundred and more than seven hundred and fifty council fathers over the course of four public sessions and about ninety general working congregations. It was the first ecumenical council since Trent, three centuries earlier, and the first to be held with the participation of bishops from every continent, a direct reflection of the Catholic missionary expansion of the nineteenth century. It took place at a time of strong tensions between the Church and the modern world: the advance of philosophical rationalism, political liberalism, and the unifying nationalism of Italy and Germany, together with the growing secularization of European societies, called into question, in the eyes of Pius IX and of a large part of the episcopate, the very foundations of traditional religious authority — a concern already expressed in 1864 in the encyclical «Quanta Cura» and in its appended «Syllabus of Errors», which condemned eighty propositions of contemporary liberal and rationalist thought.

On April 24, 1870, the council fathers unanimously approved the dogmatic constitution «Dei Filius», on the Catholic faith, which affirmed the possibility of knowing the existence of God by natural reason and the impossibility of any true contradiction between faith and reason, both coming from the same divine source. The document of greatest historical impact came on July 18, 1870: the dogmatic constitution «Pastor Aeternus», on the Church of Christ, which defined the primacy of universal jurisdiction of the Bishop of Rome over the whole Church and, in its final chapter, the dogma of papal infallibility — the pope, when he speaks «ex cathedra», that is, when exercising his office as shepherd and teacher of all Christians in order to define solemnly a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole Church, enjoys, through special divine assistance, the same infallibility with which the Church is endowed in her definitions. The definition was approved by 533 votes in favor and only two against; a larger group of bishops who disagreed with the timeliness or the formulation of the doctrine — about 55, according to estimates — preferred to leave Rome before the final vote rather than vote publicly against the wishes of the pope.

The vote on «Pastor Aeternus» coincided almost to the day with one of the most dramatic events in European politics of the century: the day after its promulgation, on July 19, 1870, the Franco-Prussian War broke out, which forced the withdrawal of the French garrison that had protected Rome for years. Without this military protection, the city became vulnerable to the advance of the troops of the Kingdom of Italy, who would occupy it on September 20 of that same year, completing Italian unification at the expense of the last remnants of the Papal States. Faced with the impossibility of guaranteeing the freedom and security of the council's work in a Rome now under Italian sovereignty, Pius IX suspended the council indefinitely on October 20, 1870.

The council was never formally reopened nor closed by a conciliar act of its own, remaining, from the juridical-canonical point of view, merely suspended — a situation without parallel in the history of the twenty-one ecumenical councils recognized by the Catholic Church. Its original agenda also foresaw a complete schema on the nature of the Church as a whole, including the relationship between the pope and the bishops, which remained pending for almost a century, revisited only with the convocation of the Second Vatican Council in 1962, whose constitution «Lumen Gentium» is seen by many theologians as the necessary complement that balances Vatican I's emphasis on papal primacy with a broader ecclesiology of episcopal collegiality.

itens.resumo: Christological formula promulgated by the Council of Chalcedon (451): in Christ, one single person subsists in two natures, divine and human, united without confusion, change, division, or separation.
itens.corpo:
The "Definition of Chalcedon" was not born of an abstract debate, but of the concrete need to resolve, in stable doctrinal language, more than a century of Christological disputes that had already divided the Church in at least two earlier great crises — the Nestorian controversy, resolved at Ephesus (431), and the Eutychian controversy, which had corrupted the so-called "Robber Council" of 449 before it was finally confronted at Chalcedon in 451. Gathered under the Emperor Marcian, the bishops present there had before them two theological traditions — that of Alexandria, more inclined to emphasize the unity of the person of Christ, and that of Antioch, more attentive to the real distinction of his two natures — which, carried to opposite extremes, had produced the heresies that the council needed to overcome without discarding what each tradition contained of truth.

Relying decisively on the "Tome of Leo," the doctrinal letter that Pope Leo the Great had sent to Bishop Flavian of Constantinople as early as 449 — and whose reading had been prevented at the "Robber Council" by the authoritarianism of Dioscorus of Alexandria — the bishops of Chalcedon produced a text of remarkable precision, still studied today as a model of balanced dogmatic definition. The formula professes Jesus Christ as "truly God and truly man," consubstantial with the Father according to the divinity and consubstantial with us according to the humanity in all things except sin, acknowledged "in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation" — the four negative adverbs that would become the classic reference for all later Christology, both Eastern and Western, precisely because they do not claim to explain the mystery of the hypostatic union positively, but only to mark out the limits within which any legitimate theological explanation must remain.

The formula sought to balance two mirror-image and opposite errors: on one side, Nestorianism, which separated the two natures of Christ so excessively as to suggest, in practice, two distinct persons coexisting in a single figure; on the other, Eutychian Monophysitism, which saw the human nature absorbed, dissolved, or confused by the divine nature after the Incarnation, like a drop of vinegar dissolved in the ocean. Against both extremes, Chalcedon affirmed that the unity of Christ is found at the level of the person (the "hypostasis"), and not at the level of nature, which remains twofold and whole, each preserving its own properties without mixing with the other.

Although accepted as a norm of definitive faith by Rome and by most of the Greek-speaking Churches of the East, the definition was rejected by important Christian communities of non-Greek tradition — most of the Coptic episcopate in Egypt, a good part of the Syrian and Armenian clergy, and later Ethiopia — who considered it dangerously close to the already condemned Nestorianism, preferring the Miaphysite formula, of Cyrilline origin, of "one nature of the incarnate Word." This refusal gave rise to the schism that still today distinguishes the so-called Oriental Orthodox Churches (Coptic, Syriac Orthodox, Armenian, Ethiopian, and Eritrean) both from Rome and from the Byzantine Orthodox Churches of Greek and Slavic tradition — a division that proved, after decades of ecumenical theological dialogue, to be more terminological and historical than properly doctrinal in its substance, as common Christological declarations signed in recent decades between the Catholic Church and several of these Eastern Churches acknowledge.

itens.titulo: Constantinople III and the Condemnation of Monothelitism
itens.resumo: Sixth ecumenical council (680-681): it defined that Christ possesses two natural wills and two natural operations, divine and human, condemning Monoenergism and Monothelitism and, by name, Pope Honorius I for having tolerated them.
itens.corpo:
The root of Monothelitism goes back to the beginning of the seventh century, when the Emperor Heraclius, seeking to reconcile the Chalcedonian Churches with the Miaphysite communities of Egypt and Syria — territories he had just reconquered from the Persians and would soon lose to the Arabs —, supported a compromise formula proposed by Patriarch Sergius I of Constantinople: first Monoenergism, according to which Christ would have a single «energy» or operation; then, when that formula proved theologically untenable, Monothelitism proper, according to which Christ, although possessing two natures as Chalcedon had defined, would have a single will, the divine one. Heraclius consolidated this compromise position in the decree «Ecthesis» (638), and his successor Constans II tried to impose silence on the question with the edict «Typos» (648-649), which in practice suppressed the orthodox doctrine.

The firmest and most influential theological opponent of this position was the Palestinian monk Maximus the Confessor, who argued with great philosophical rigor that denying Christ a distinct and active human will compromised the real integrity of his humanity — for a human nature without a will of its own would not be a complete human nature, but only a passive instrument of the divine will. For his stubborn resistance, Maximus was tried, had his tongue cut out and his right hand amputated by imperial order, to prevent him from preaching or writing against the official doctrine, and he died in exile in the Caucasus region in 662, decades before seeing his position triumph.

The preparation for the council was careful. After the Emperor Constantine IV overcame the Muslim siege of Constantinople in 678, he wrote to Pope Donus proposing a conference on the question; Donus had already died, and his successor, Agatho, welcomed the proposal, ordering consultations throughout the West — there was a synod in Milan, under Archbishop Mansuetus, another in Hatfield (680), presided over by Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury, and a synod in Rome at Easter of 680, with 125 Italian bishops, which composed a profession of faith condemning Monothelitism, carried to Constantinople by the papal legates in early September 680.

On September 10, 680, the emperor published an edict ordering the convocation of the council. It opened on November 7, in the domed hall of the imperial palace called the «Trullo» — from which the council's alternative name, «Trullan», derives — and held 18 sessions, presided over by the emperor in the first eleven. At the opening session there were only 37 bishops and a few presbyters; the number grew to about 300 over the course of the proceedings, but the final acts bear 174 signatures. The Patriarchs of Constantinople and Antioch took part in person; Alexandria and Jerusalem, without patriarchs because of the Muslim conquest, were represented by prelates appointed by Byzantium. Read in the second session, Agatho's long dogmatic letter and the document of the Roman synod insisted on the faith of the Apostolic See as the living and unblemished tradition of the Apostles, guaranteed by the promises of Christ. On March 7, 681, in the eighth session, the council adopted the teaching of Agatho; Macarius of Antioch was almost the only one to refuse assent and was eventually deposed in the twelfth session, together with his supporters.

Relying above all on the argumentation that Maximus had developed decades earlier — whose name, however, the council avoided mentioning, since he was still viewed with suspicion —, the council defined, in the seventeenth session, that two natural wills and two natural operations, divine and human, belong to Christ, «without division, without change, without separation, without confusion», and that Christ's human will, although in full subjection to the divine, was neither suppressed nor absorbed. The definition was promulgated in the eighteenth and final session, on September 16, 681, and the acts, signed by 174 fathers and by the emperor himself, were sent to Pope Leo II — who had succeeded Agatho, dead before receiving the acts — for confirmation.

The episode is also remembered for an uncomfortable page of papal history: the council included by name, among those anathematized, Pope Honorius I himself, dead about half a century earlier, for his correspondence with Sergius of Constantinople (c. 634), in which he seemed to tacitly accept the formula of a single will in Christ. The condemnation was ratified by Leo II when he confirmed the conciliar acts, but Leo II himself attributed the censure to Honorius's pastoral negligence — who, according to his formula, «did not extinguish, as befitted the apostolic dignity, the flame of the heretical dogma that was beginning, but fed it by neglecting it» —, and not to a personal and deliberate profession of heresy. The case, one of the few in which an ecumenical council censured a successor of Peter posthumously, is studied with particular care by the theology of the limits of papal infallibility, since Honorius had spoken in a private letter, and not «ex cathedra» — a distinction that would become central in the preparatory debates of the First Vatican Council itself, in 1870.

itens.titulo: Nicaea II and the Veneration of Sacred Images
itens.resumo: The Second Council of Nicaea (787) brought to an end the first phase of the Byzantine iconoclast controversy, defining that sacred images may be venerated, but not adored, since adoration is due to God alone.
itens.corpo:
The iconoclast controversy that Nicaea II would bring to an end in its first phase began around 726-730, when the Emperor Leo III the Isaurian, possibly influenced by theological currents of the Near East hostile to any representation of the divine, and relying on a rigorist reading of the biblical commandment against idolatry, began an official policy of removing and destroying religious icons throughout the Byzantine Empire. His son Constantine V radicalized this policy in a systematic way, convening in 754 a council gathered in the palace of Hieria — without any representation of the patriarchates of Rome, Alexandria, Antioch or Jerusalem — which formally condemned the production and cult of sacred images as a form of idolatry, unleashing decades of persecution against monks and clerics who resisted the systematic destruction of icons in churches and monasteries.

The turning point came with the death of the Emperor Leo IV in 780, and the rise of his widow, Irene, as empress-regent in the name of her minor son. Irene, a venerator of images, carefully orchestrated the return to iconodule orthodoxy, appointing to the patriarchate of Constantinople a layman she trusted, Tarasius, who accepted the office on the condition that a new ecumenical council be convened. Finally assembled at Nicaea in 787, after a first failed attempt in Constantinople the previous year, the council had about 350 participants, most of them Eastern bishops, with legates of Pope Adrian I, who fully confirmed its decisions.

The core of Nicaea II's doctrinal contribution was the precise distinction between two kinds of religious honor that the iconoclast controversy had dangerously confused: the "veneration" (in Greek, "proskýnesis") due to the images of Christ, of Our Lady, of the angels and of the saints — comparable, in nature, to the honor traditionally paid to the cross, to the book of the Gospels and to other sacred objects — and the "adoration" ("latreia"), which is due exclusively to God, under pain of idolatry. The council explained this distinction with an argument of remarkable simplicity: whoever venerates an image pays homage, through it, to the person represented in it, and not to the painted panel, the paint or the pigment of which it is made — the material support is merely a vehicle, never the final object, of religious veneration.

Nicaea II further defined, in positive terms, that it is fitting and proper to place sacred images in churches, on vessels and liturgical vestments, on walls, fabrics and even in the private homes of the faithful, recognizing the catechetical and devotional value of images for a largely illiterate population, for whom icons functioned as a true "Bible of the poor" in visual form. This doctrinal foundation is still invoked today by the Catholic Church — and also by the Orthodox Churches, for which the question of icons carries even greater theological weight — to justify the use of images, statues and icons both in the official liturgy and in popular devotion, always distinguishing, as Nicaea II did, between honoring a representation and adoring that which is due to God alone.

The definition of 787 did not put an end to the controversy once and for all: the Byzantine Empire would live through a second iconoclast period between 815 and 843, under new emperors hostile to images, overcome only with the so-called "Triumph of Orthodoxy" in 843, when the empress-regent Theodora definitively restored the cult of images — an episode that the Byzantine liturgy celebrates to this day on the first Sunday of Lent as a symbolic landmark of the final victory of the iconodule faith.

itens.resumo: Promulgated at the sixth session of the Council of Trent (1547), the decree sets out the Catholic doctrine on how the sinner is justified before God, in direct response to the Lutheran doctrine of justification by faith alone; it consists of a preamble, sixteen chapters and thirty-three canons.
itens.corpo:
When the conciliar fathers of Trent turned to the subject of justification, three decades had already passed since Martin Luther, in 1517, made public his central thesis that the human being is justified before God "by faith alone" ("sola fide") — not by the cooperation of good works, which Luther saw as incapable of contributing in any measure to salvation, obtained solely by grace imputed externally to the sinner by virtue of the merits of Christ. After failed attempts at theological reconciliation, such as the Colloquy of Regensburg (1541), the question of justification had become the most urgent and most technically complex point of the entire controversy between Rome and the Reformation.

Convened under Pope Paul III on January 13, 1547, and presided over in the pontiff's name by the cardinal legates Giovanni Maria del Monte, Bishop of Palestrina, and Marcello Cervini, the sixth session of the council produced, after months of intense theological debate among the conciliar fathers themselves — who disagreed internally over important nuances of the question —, the longest and most elaborate doctrinal document of the entire Council of Trent. The decree is structured in a preamble, sixteen expository chapters and thirty-three condemnatory canons. Against the Lutheran formula of justification by faith alone, it teaches that justification is the sovereign work of God's grace, which first precedes and then accompanies the free response of the human person, so that there is no prior human merit that provokes it, but neither is there justification without some form of free cooperation of the human will with this freely offered grace. Faith, the decree teaches, is truly the "beginning, foundation and root" of all justification, but it must express itself and grow in hope and charity — and in the good works that flow from it — in order to remain alive and not stay barren; justification, the following chapter affirms, does not consist merely in the forgiveness of sins, but also in the interior renewal wrought by the Holy Spirit, who infuses the theological virtues of faith, hope and charity into the soul of the justified.

The decree further affirms, in a point of sharp divergence from Protestant currents that taught the absolute and subjective assurance of one's own salvation ("certainty of election"), that the justification received can indeed be lost through grave mortal sin, and recovered through the sacrament of Penance by means of contrition, confession and satisfaction — so that no Christian, according to Trent, can have absolute and infallible certainty of his own state of grace, save by special revelation. The document closes with the thirty-three canons that condemn, in brief and direct formulas ("si quis dixerit... anathema sit", "if anyone says... let him be anathema"), specific propositions then attributed to the various currents of the Reformation on the subject, from the denial of human free will to the idea that the good works of the justified would be, in themselves, sinful.

The Tridentine decree on justification remained, for more than four centuries, one of the points of greatest doctrinal division between Catholicism and Lutheranism, until decades of bilateral ecumenical dialogue resulted in the "Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification," signed in Augsburg on October 31, 1999, by the Lutheran bishop Christian Krause, then president of the Lutheran World Federation, and by Cardinal Edward I. Cassidy, representative of the Holy See. The document recognized a possible consensus on the fundamental truths of the doctrine of justification — "by grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work and not because of any merit on our part, we are accepted by God," proclaims its central formula —, though without eliminating all the remaining differences of emphasis and theological language between the traditions. In 2006 the World Methodist Council endorsed the declaration; in 2016 and 2017 the Anglican Communion and the World Communion of Reformed Churches followed. The consensus, however, was not unanimous: more conservative Lutherans, such as the Missouri Synod, rejected the document, and in 2015 the International Lutheran Council also rejected it, on the grounds that Rome has not revised the doctrinal decisions of the Council of Trent.

itens.titulo: Trent: Decree on the Most Holy Eucharist
itens.resumo: In its thirteenth session (October 11, 1551), the Council of Trent dogmatically defined the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist and established the term "transubstantiation" to describe the conversion of the bread and wine, formulating eleven canons condemning the positions of the Reformers. The question of communion under both kinds would only be settled ten years later, in Session XXI.
itens.corpo:
Among the different Protestant positions on the nature of the Lord's Supper that divided the Reformers among themselves, the sixteenth century saw a broad spectrum of opinions emerge: from the virtually complete denial of any real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, upheld by Huldrych Zwingli, for whom the bread and wine were merely symbolic memorials, through the intermediate position of John Calvin, who admitted a real spiritual but not bodily presence, to the so-called "consubstantiation" of Martin Luther, who maintained a strong belief in the real presence of Christ but rejected the scholastic philosophical explanation that the substance of the bread ceased to exist — Luther, who did not deny the real presence, saw in "transubstantiation" an undue interference of Aristotelian philosophy in the revealed datum. Faced with this doctrinal fragmentation, the Council of Trent needed not only to reaffirm the traditional faith, but to do so with enough terminological precision to distinguish the Catholic position from all these alternatives.

Held on October 11, 1551, already under Pope Julius III — Trent had been temporarily suspended between 1547 and 1551 because of political disputes, disputes over precedence between the Spanish and Italian delegations, and an outbreak of typhus — the thirteenth session of the council was the third convened under Julius III and responded to these different positions by reaffirming that, by the consecration of the bread and wine during the Mass, there takes place the conversion of the whole substance of the bread into the substance of the Body of Christ and of the whole substance of the wine into the substance of his Blood, with only the sensible appearances ("species") of bread and wine remaining — color, taste, texture, weight —, none of which remains attached to the original substance. The decree expressly declares that this conversion is "aptly and properly called transubstantiation by the Catholic Church," crystallizing into official dogmatic terminology a technical vocabulary that medieval scholastic theology, above all Saint Thomas Aquinas in his "Summa Theologiae" (III, q. 75), had been developing and refining for more than three centuries, and which the Fourth Lateran Council, in 1215, had itself already employed in a conciliar document. The text of Trent also enumerates the three terms with which the Catholic faith has always professed the Eucharistic presence — "true, real and substantial" —, distinguishing it both from a merely figurative presence and from a simply "dynamic" or spiritual presence.

To the dogmatic decree — which comprises doctrinal chapters and the definition of transubstantiation —, the council appended eleven canons of condemnation, closed by the formula "let him be anathema." They follow and condemn, point by point, the principal Protestant positions: the denial that the Body and Blood of Christ are truly, really and substantially present, with the soul and the divinity (against Zwingli, canon 1); the assertion that the substance of the bread and wine coexists with the Body and Blood — the Lutheran position — attacked in canon 2, which denies that "admirabilis et singularis conversio" which the Church aptly calls "transubstantiation"; the denial that Christ is present whole and entire under each of the two species separately and under any portion of them, even the smallest particle (canon 3), a point that underlies the Catholic practice of dividing a consecrated host into pieces without this multiplying, dividing or fragmenting the integral presence of Christ in each part; the reduction of Christ's presence to the moment of reception alone, denying it in the hosts kept after communion (canon 4); the rejection of reservation and of carrying the Eucharist to the sick (canon 7); the denial of sacramental and real communion, beyond the "spiritual" (canon 8); in addition to canons 9, 10 and 11, on the obligation to receive communion at least at Easter, the communion of the celebrating priest and the fruits of the sacrament.

The same session also approved a "Decree on Reform" (only the dogmatic decree on the Eucharist had been planned for that date), and notable theologians and prelates attended it — among the participants in the Tridentine debates were the cardinal and future Archbishop of Milan Charles Borromeo, nephew of Pius IV, and the Jesuits Diego Laínez and Alfonso Salmerón, first companions of Ignatius of Loyola, whose presence marks the rise of the Society of Jesus as a theological force of the Counter-Reformation. It is important to note that the decree of Session XIII did not exhaust the Eucharistic theme: the question of communion under both kinds — that is, whether the chalice should be offered to the laity — was only settled ten years later, in Session XXI (July 16, 1562), under Pius IV. There the council declared that the laity and non-celebrating clerics are not bound by divine precept to receive communion under both forms and that communion under one species suffices for salvation, while acknowledging, however, that "from the beginning of the Christian religion the use of both species was common," but that this custom "changed widely with time" — an argument from the Church's authority over the administration of the sacraments, which would be taken up again in the twentieth century to justify the partial restoration of the chalice to the laity.

The Tridentine decree on the Eucharist remains, more than four and a half centuries later, the central and still binding dogmatic reference of Catholic doctrine on the subject, cited directly or indirectly in practically every catechesis and every subsequent magisterial document on the real presence of Christ in the Eucharistic sacrament. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992), in setting out this doctrine in the numbers dealing with the sacrament, takes up the definition of Trent literally, and the concept of "transubstantiation" continues to be the official expression with which the Church formulates the mystery of the Eucharistic conversion.

itens.resumo: Dogmatic constitution of the First Vatican Council, promulgated by Pius IX on April 24, 1870: it affirms that God can be known with certainty by the natural light of reason from created things, and that faith and reason, coming from the same God, can never truly contradict each other.
itens.corpo:
Promulgated on April 24, 1870, almost three months before the more famous «Pastor Aeternus», the dogmatic constitution «Dei Filius» was the first major doctrinal document of the First Vatican Council (1869-1870), the twentieth ecumenical council and the first to meet in Saint Peter's Basilica. The council had been convoked by Pius IX on June 29, 1868 and opened on December 8, 1869, with about 700 prelates present out of roughly 1,050 eligible bishops. «Dei Filius» responded to a set of philosophical currents that, in the assessment of the pope and of the majority of the assembled episcopate, threatened the rational and supernatural foundations of the Christian faith: rationalism, which reduced all truth to the exclusive reach of reason; materialism, which denied any spiritual reality; pantheism, then influential above all through German idealist currents, which identified God with the universe itself; and traditionalism and fideism, which denied to human reason any autonomous capacity to know fundamental religious truths without the direct support of revelation or tradition.

The editorial history of the document reveals the internal tensions of the council. The preparatory work, directed by a central commission and subcommissions dominated by the Curia, produced 51 schemas, of which only 6 actually reached the plenary assembly. The first schema on the faith, distributed to the council fathers in December 1869, was rejected as obscure, prolix, polemical and tied to an outdated vocabulary — more a learned treatise by a university professor than a conciliar text. A «deputation on the faith» was charged with preparing a new draft, and the text was rewritten by the Jesuit Joseph Kleutgen, with the collaboration of Bishops Dechamps, Pie and Martin. The new version, much shorter, was presented on March 18, 1870 and discussed until April 6; on April 12 it was approved with 515 «placet» votes and no «non placet», but with 83 «placet iuxta modum» votes requesting revisions, above all regarding the opening words of chapter I. In the final vote of April 24, all 667 members present voted «placet».

The title of the constitution, taken from its opening words, once raised a significant controversy. A group of 35 English-speaking bishops feared that the expression «Sancta Romana Catholica Ecclesia» («Holy Roman Catholic Church») could be read as favorable to the Anglican «branch theory», and proposed removing the adjective «Romana». The proposal was widely rejected, but, in consideration of the reservations expressed, the final text ended up reordering the terms and adding «Apostolica», so that it reads «Sancta Catholica Apostolica Romana Ecclesia».

The text is organized into four chapters with corresponding canons. The first teaches that God, the principle and end of all things, «can be known with certainty by the natural light of human reason from created things» (cf. Rom 1), establishing the doctrinal basis of a genuine natural theology, taking up a line that goes back to Saint Thomas Aquinas and his «five ways». The second chapter deals with revelation, affirming its necessity both for knowing the strict mysteries of the faith — Trinity, Incarnation — and so that religious truths that are in principle accessible to reason may be known with ease, certainty and without error. The third chapter deals with the nature and conditions of faith as a free and rational act. The fourth, on faith and reason, contains the most quoted formulation: «even though faith is above reason, there can never be any real disagreement between faith and reason, since the same God who reveals the mysteries and infuses faith has also endowed the human mind with the light of reason, and God cannot deny himself, nor can truth ever contradict truth».

This principle of harmony — not of identity, but of no real contradiction between the natural and the supernatural order — continues to guide Catholic reflection on science and faith, and is explicitly taken up in later documents, such as the conciliar constitution «Dei Verbum» (1965), which presented itself as continuing Trent and Vatican I, and the encyclical «Fides et Ratio» (1998) of John Paul II. The council, which was never formally dissolved, had its sessions suspended indefinitely by Pius IX on October 20, 1870, after the troops of the Kingdom of Italy occupied Rome on September 20, in the context of the Franco-Prussian War — leaving a good part of the originally planned program unfinished.
